name: Meniscus Tear
secondary_queries: can a torn meniscus heal on its own
seo_title: Meniscus Tear Treatment Palm Beach Gardens | ELITE
seo_desc: Torn meniscus care in Palm Beach Gardens and Port St. Lucie, from rest and rehab to arthroscopic meniscus repair, with board-certified surgeon Dr. Matarazzo.
lede: A torn meniscus can make your knee catch, swell or ache when you twist. Many tears settle with rest and rehab, and some are best repaired.
what_it_is: Each knee has two menisci, wedge-shaped pads of tough fibrocartilage that sit between the thighbone and the shinbone. One lies on the inner side of the knee and one on the outer side. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) describes them as shock absorbers that help pass your body weight through the joint and keep it steady. Tears are named by their shape, such as flap, radial or bucket handle tears.

Two groups tend to tear a meniscus. Younger, active people often do it with a forceful pivot or cut during contact sports, sometimes alongside an ACL injury. Older adults are more likely to have a degenerative tear, where tissue weakened by age gives way with very little force. The AAOS notes that an awkward twist while getting up from a chair can be enough. Meniscus tears happen at every age, so a sports history is not required.
symptoms: A pop felt at the moment of injury
Pain along the inner or outer side of the knee
Catching or locking, as if something is stuck in the joint
A feeling that the knee may give way
Trouble fully straightening or bending the leg
causes: Pivoting or cutting with the foot planted
Contact sports and sports with sudden direction changes
Age-related wear that weakens the meniscus
An awkward twist during an everyday movement
A coexisting ACL tear or knee arthritis

how_therapy_helps.intro: The AAOS and Mayo Clinic both describe nonsurgical care as a sensible starting point for many tears. Rest, ice, anti-inflammatory medicine and a strengthening program often calm symptoms, and Mayo Clinic notes that many tears that do not lock the knee become less painful over time. Dr. Matarazzo looks at the tear's type and location, your age and activity level, and whether the knee mechanically locks. When surgery makes sense, repair is favored for tissue with a chance to heal, and trimming is reserved for pieces that cannot.
methods: Avoiding twisting and pivoting for a while, sometimes with crutches, gives an irritated knee time to settle.
Physical therapy builds the thigh and hip muscles that support the knee, which Mayo Clinic notes can help stabilize the joint after a tear.
Anti-inflammatory medicine or a corticosteroid injection can ease pain and swelling, particularly when a degenerative tear sits in a knee that also has arthritis.
Arthroscopic stitching of the torn edges aims to keep the meniscus working as a shock absorber. Mayo Clinic notes that repair is sometimes possible, especially in children and younger adults.
When a torn flap cannot heal and keeps catching, the damaged portion is trimmed through small incisions while keeping as much healthy meniscus as possible.

first_visit: Dr. Matarazzo will ask how the injury happened, whether you felt a pop and whether the knee catches or locks. He presses along the joint line for tenderness, watches you walk and squat, and may perform the McMurray test, which bends, straightens and rotates the knee. X-rays help rule out arthritis or fracture because they cannot show the meniscus itself. An MRI, which Mayo Clinic calls the best imaging study for a torn meniscus, may follow.
recovery: Recovery depends on the treatment. According to the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, recovery after a partial meniscectomy takes about 3 to 6 weeks, and many people can put weight on the leg right away. A meniscus repair takes longer, about 3 to 6 months, because the stitched tissue needs protection while it heals. Nonsurgical recovery varies widely with the size and type of tear. Sticking with the prescribed exercises matters in every case, and your own timeline may be faster or slower.
self_care: Avoid twisting and pivoting while the knee is sore.
Ice for about 15 minutes at a time to manage swelling.
Use a compression sleeve and keep the leg elevated when you sit.
Over-the-counter pain relievers can help if they are safe for you.
Use crutches if walking makes the pain worse.
see_a_doctor: The knee locks and will not straighten
You cannot put weight on the leg
Heavy swelling soon after an injury
Fever with redness or warmth around the knee
Pain, swelling or a bluish color in the calf
No improvement after three days of home care

faqs.q: Can a torn meniscus heal on its own?
faqs.a: Some meniscus tears improve without surgery. Mayo Clinic notes that many tears that do not lock the knee become less painful over time, and tears linked to arthritis often settle as the arthritis is treated. Whether the torn tissue itself heals depends on where and how it tore. A knee that keeps catching, locking or swelling deserves an exam rather than more waiting.

faqs.q: Do I need surgery for a meniscus tear?
faqs.a: Not always. Many tears are first treated with rest, ice, medication and a strengthening program. According to Mayo Clinic, surgery is generally considered when the knee locks or when symptoms continue despite nonsurgical care. Your age, the tear pattern, your activity goals and any arthritis in the knee all shape whether surgery is likely to help.

faqs.q: What is the difference between meniscus repair and meniscectomy?
faqs.a: A meniscus repair stitches the torn pieces back together so the meniscus can keep cushioning the knee. A partial meniscectomy trims away the torn portion that cannot heal. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons notes that meniscectomy allows a quicker return, while repair requires a longer, more protected recovery because the tissue has to knit together.

faqs.q: What does a torn meniscus feel like?
faqs.a: People describe pain along the inside or outside of the knee, swelling and stiffness, and sometimes a pop when the tear happened. A common clue is catching or locking, where the knee seems to stick until you wiggle it free. Some people feel the knee give way. Symptoms can be mild with small degenerative tears and sharper after a sports injury.

faqs.q: Do you need an MRI to diagnose a meniscus tear?
faqs.a: A doctor can often suspect a meniscus tear from your history and exam, including tenderness along the joint line and tests that rotate the knee. Mayo Clinic describes MRI as the best imaging study to detect a torn meniscus, and it helps plan treatment when surgery is being considered. X-rays cannot show the meniscus but help rule out arthritis or fracture.

faqs.q: Is a meniscus tear common in older adults?
faqs.a: Yes. The American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons explains that the meniscus wears with age, which makes degenerative tears more common in older adults. These tears can happen with very little force, such as twisting while getting up from a chair. They often appear alongside early arthritis, which affects how they are treated, and many respond to nonsurgical care.
